items.title: 1. How respiratory failure develops
items.body:
## 1.1 Why gas exchange fails

![Three determinants of gas exchange failure](set3-fig1.png)

The respiratory system performs two different jobs. **Oxygenation** loads oxygen from alveolar gas into pulmonary capillary blood; **ventilation** eliminates metabolic CO₂. A patient may fail either job, or both. Starting with this distinction prevents the common error of assuming that a normal saturation excludes serious ventilatory failure.

**Alveolar ventilation:**

- PaCO₂ ≈ 0.863 × V̇CO₂ / V̇A when V̇CO₂ is in mL/min, alveolar ventilation in L/min, and PaCO₂ in mmHg. V̇A = (VT − VD) × f.
- Thus CO₂ accumulates when tidal volume becomes small, physiological dead space increases, or respiratory rate cannot compensate.
- A higher minute ventilation does not necessarily mean higher effective alveolar ventilation: rapid shallow breaths waste a larger fraction in dead space.

**Oxygenation:**

- The simplified alveolar gas equation at sea level is PAO₂ ≈ FiO₂(Patm − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/R, with R ≈ 0.8.
- On room air at sea level, PAO₂ ≈ 150 − PaCO₂/0.8 mmHg. The **A–a gradient** (PAO₂ − PaO₂) distinguishes pure hypoventilation from intrinsic oxygen-transfer abnormalities.
- It normally rises with age and FiO₂; an approximate room-air reference is (age/4)+4 mmHg, but it is not a universal diagnostic threshold.

| **Mechanism** | **Physiological problem** | **Expected O₂ response** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low inspired O₂ | Reduced alveolar PO₂ | Usually responds to higher FiO₂ | Altitude, oxygen supply error |
| Alveolar hypoventilation | ↑ PaCO₂ lowers PAO₂; near-normal A–a gradient if lungs otherwise normal | Oxygen corrects saturation but **not** CO₂ accumulation | Opioid overdose, neuromuscular weakness |
| V/Q mismatch | Perfused poorly ventilated units; low V/Q regions dominate arterial hypoxaemia | Often responsive to oxygen | COPD, asthma, pneumonia, atelectasis |
| True right-to-left shunt | Venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli; increased shunt fraction | Relatively refractory to oxygen; needs recruitment or correction | Consolidated lung, severe ARDS, intracardiac shunt |
| Diffusion limitation | Thickened/low surface-area alveolocapillary barrier; worse with short transit time | Responds to O₂ | ILD, emphysema, exercise |
| Increased dead space | Ventilated but poorly perfused lung; wasted ventilation; CO₂ may rise | Does not imply primary hypoxaemia | PE, low cardiac output, excessive PEEP |

- **Clinical pearl:** If PaO₂ remains low on FiO₂ 1.0, think major shunt, profound V/Q mismatch, oxygen-system failure or an intracardiac right-to-left shunt. Increasing FiO₂ further cannot fix a ventilator with disconnected oxygen supply or reopen consolidated alveoli.

**Oxygen delivery is different from PaO₂.** DO₂ = cardiac output × CaO₂; CaO₂ ≈ 1.34 × Hb(g/dL) × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂. The oxygen bound to haemoglobin dominates. A patient can have SpO₂ 100% but inadequate DO₂ from severe anaemia or circulatory failure. Conversely, pulse oximetry does not measure CO₂, ventilation or cardiac output.

## 1.2 Type I versus type II respiratory failure

| **Characteristic** | **Type I: hypoxaemic** | **Type II: hypercapnic** |
|---|---|---|
| Working definition | PaO₂ <8 kPa (60 mmHg) on room air, with PaCO₂ normal/low in a pure case | PaCO₂ >6 kPa (45 mmHg), often with hypoxaemia; respiratory acidosis establishes acute ventilatory failure |
| Mechanism | Shunt, V/Q mismatch, impaired diffusion or low FiO₂ | Inadequate effective alveolar ventilation relative to CO₂ production |
| Frequent causes | Pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, PE, atelectasis | COPD, severe asthma, obesity hypoventilation, CNS depression, neuromuscular weakness, chest-wall restriction |
| Common bedside clues | Tachypnoea, ↑ work, refractory SpO₂ | Somnolence, headache, tremor, asterixis, muscle fatigue; may be tachypnoeic or bradypnoeic |
| First principle | Correct oxygenation and underlying lung lesion | Support alveolar ventilation and treat cause, **while ensuring oxygenation** |

These are **overlapping physiological patterns**, not separate diagnoses. A patient with COPD and pneumonia can have severe shunt plus acute hypercapnia; a patient with massive PE can have hypoxaemia and high dead space but an initially low PaCO₂ from hyperventilation. Hypercapnia usually develops later when compensatory ventilation is exhausted.

## 1.3 Acute, chronic and acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure

In **acute hypercapnia**, renal bicarbonate compensation has not occurred. Roughly, HCO₃⁻ increases about 1 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg rise in PaCO₂ in an acute respiratory acidosis, versus ≈3.5–4 mmol/L per 10 mmHg when chronically compensated. These are interpretation heuristics, not formulas for prescribing bicarbonate.

- **Worked interpretation:** ABG pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 9.0 kPa (68 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 27 mmol/L suggests acute respiratory acidosis. pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 8.5 kPa (64 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 34 suggests chronic CO₂ retention. pH 7.18, PaCO₂ 9.5 kPa and HCO₃⁻ 27 in someone usually compensated suggests acute-on-chronic failure, particularly if baseline HCO₃⁻ was 34.

- Acute respiratory failure threatens rapid exhaustion, hypoxic brain injury and dysrhythmia.
- Chronic failure allows renal compensation and adaptive changes but introduces oxygen sensitivity, pulmonary hypertension, polycythaemia and deconditioning.
- **Treat the physiology and trajectory rather than normalising a long-standing PaCO₂ abruptly:** severe rapid correction can produce alkalemia and neurological symptoms, while generous oxygen without ventilatory support can worsen hypercapnia in vulnerable COPD/OHS patients.

## 1.4 Clinical assessment and severity

- Start by identifying whether the patient can maintain the airway, sustain breathing and perfuse the brain.
- **Impending arrest** is signalled by deteriorating consciousness, exhaustion, silent chest, paradoxical breathing, inability to speak, ineffective cough, profound hypoxaemia despite support, haemodynamic instability or rapidly worsening acidosis; do not wait for a particular PaCO₂ value.

- A focused assessment asks: When did it begin?
- Is the problem oxygenation, ventilation, airway protection or circulation?
- What is the reversible trigger?
- Seek infection/aspiration, pulmonary oedema, PE, pneumothorax, drugs/opioids, COPD/asthma, residual neuromuscular block, thoracic/neurological injury, obesity hypoventilation and chronic neuromuscular disease.
- Examine rate, work and pattern of breathing, chest expansion, breath sounds, stridor/wheeze, percussion, JVP, oedema, temperature, mental status and cough strength.

**Useful investigations, selected by stability:**

- Arterial blood gas with FiO₂ and time
- CXR or lung ultrasound
- ECG
- FBC, electrolytes/renal function, lactate, glucose and infection studies
- Troponin/BNP when cardiac disease suspected
- D-dimer/CTPA only within appropriate PE pathways
- Focused echo for LV/RV/tamponade
- Pleural ultrasound for pneumothorax/effusion.
- In severe instability, treat immediately and use bedside ultrasound/echo rather than hazardous transfer for CT.

## 1.5 Interpreting ABG, CXR and PFTs in respiratory failure

**ABG sequence:**

- (1) confirm sampling and FiO₂
- (2) check pH
- (3) identify primary PaCO₂ or bicarbonate disorder
- (4) check expected compensation
- (5) examine PaO₂ against FiO₂ and calculate P/F (PaO₂ / FiO₂)
- (6) inspect lactate, haemoglobin, potassium and coexisting metabolic disturbance.
- Example: PaO₂ 8 kPa on FiO₂ 0.6 → 60/0.6 = **P/F 100 mmHg**; severe oxygenation failure even though an isolated PaO₂ of 8 kPa might look modest.

**Chest imaging patterns:**

- Bilateral fluffy infiltrates with congestion/effusions suggest hydrostatic oedema
- Patchy bilateral opacities with a trigger and no predominant hydrostatic cause suggest ARDS
- Focal lobar air-space disease with air bronchograms supports pneumonia
- Volume loss with fissure/mediastinal displacement suggests atelectasis
- Peripheral lucency/no pleural lung markings suggests pneumothorax.
- Portable supine CXR can miss anterior pneumothorax and has substantial overlap between patterns: integrate ultrasound and physiology.

**Lung ultrasound** (Kim and Lau, ANZCA Blue Book 2025):

- Anterior sliding and horizontal A-lines support aerated lung.
- Multiple B-lines show interstitial syndrome but are not specific for heart failure.
- Focal consolidation with dynamic air bronchograms favours pneumonia.
- No lung sliding may reflect pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, pleural adhesions or apnoea.
- A **lung point is highly specific** for pneumothorax if seen, but absence cannot exclude it.

- Integrate findings with the clinical context and scan multiple zones.

**Spirometry:**

- FEV₁/FVC below the lower limit of normal (or post-bronchodilator <0.70 in GOLD COPD criteria) indicates obstruction; a low FVC with preserved/increased ratio suggests restriction but requires **TLC below LLN** for confirmation.
- In obstruction, the flow–volume expiratory limb is concave and RV/TLC may rise from trapping; in restriction, the loop is smaller but shape often preserved.
- Bronchodilator reversibility supports variable airflow limitation, but does not make COPD impossible.
- DLCO falls in emphysema, ILD and pulmonary vascular disease; may be preserved/increased in asthma or alveolar haemorrhage.

| **Parameter** | **Obstructive (COPD/asthma)** | **Restrictive (ILD/neuromuscular)** | **Clinical use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| FEV₁/FVC | Reduced | Normal/high | Obstruction versus suspected restriction |
| TLC | Normal/high with hyperinflation | Reduced in true restriction | Confirm restriction |
| RV/TLC | Increased with air trapping | Can increase in muscle weakness, varies in ILD | Risk of dynamic hyperinflation |
| DLCO | Low in emphysema, often normal in asthma | Often low in parenchymal ILD; may be relatively preserved in pure chest-wall restriction | Gas exchange reserve and diffusion severity |
| MIP/MEP, VC upright/supine | Not usually primary abnormality | Reduced in neuromuscular weakness; supine fall suggests diaphragm weakness | Identify hypoventilation/cough risk |

- **Why this matters for the viva:** “FEV₁ 45% predicted” tells you severity of airflow obstruction, but not whether the patient has an active infection, exercise intolerance, pulmonary hypertension, severe dynamic hyperinflation or an acute indication to cancel surgery. Combine tests with functional capacity, exacerbation history, oxygen use and examination.

### Reading flow–volume loops: a graphical approach (SS_IC 1.43)

- A flow–volume loop plots **flow (vertical axis, L/s)** against **volume (horizontal axis, L)**.
- Expiration is conventionally above the horizontal axis and inspiration below it; direction of volume change depends on the laboratory's plotting convention.
- A forced expiration starts near total lung capacity (TLC), rapidly reaches **peak expiratory flow (PEF)** and then falls to zero as the patient approaches residual volume (RV).
- The width of the expiratory limb represents the **forced vital capacity (FVC)**.
- **FEV₁ is a volume exhaled in the first second:** it is obtained from the accompanying volume–time curve, not directly read as a single point from the loop.
- Always verify acceptable effort, reproducibility and the displayed axes before interpreting a tracing.

![Flow–volume loop patterns](set3-fig2.png)

Schematic flow–volume loops showing normal, obstructive, restrictive, and upper-airway obstruction patterns (original teaching schematic)

| **Pattern** | **Shape of the loop** | **Interpretation and important trap** |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Rapid rise to PEF, smooth nearly linear descending expiratory limb; rounded inspiration | Curve varies with effort and age; first establish technical quality. |
| Obstructive (COPD/asthma) | Reduced PEF with a **scooped/concave expiratory limb**; often reduced FEV₁/FVC | Expiratory flow limitation, air trapping; mild obstruction can exist without a dramatic scoop. Asthma may improve after bronchodilator. |
| Restrictive (fibrosis, chest-wall disease) | **Small, narrow volume loop**, often relatively preserved shape; FEV₁ and FVC fall together | A small FVC suggests restriction but does **not** prove it. Confirm TLC below lower limit of normal (LLN); air trapping can also reduce FVC. |
| Fixed central airway obstruction (stenosis) | Plateau/flattening of **both inspiratory and expiratory limbs** | Consider tracheal stenosis, fixed lesion or a large mass; further evaluation may require CT, flexible bronchoscopy and airway planning. |
| Variable extrathoracic obstruction | **Inspiratory limb flattened** more than expiratory | Negative intraluminal pressure on inspiration narrows a compliant extrathoracic segment; e.g. vocal-fold dysfunction. |
| Variable intrathoracic obstruction | **Expiratory limb flattened** more than inspiratory | Positive pleural pressure compresses a collapsible intrathoracic large airway on forced expiration; variable tumour/tracheomalacia. |

**Interpret spirometry together with measured lung volumes and gas transfer:**

- An FEV₁/FVC below the LLN (often z < −1.645) identifies an obstructive physiological pattern using ERS/ATS interpretative standards.
- GOLD's post-bronchodilator fixed ratio <0.70 is a separate COPD diagnostic convention that can overdiagnose obstruction in older adults and underdiagnose it in younger adults.
- A low FVC with a preserved ratio is not proof of restriction: TLC must be measured.
- If both FEV₁/FVC and TLC are below LLN, the pattern is **mixed**.
- DLCO (haemoglobin-corrected where possible) may be reduced in emphysema, ILD, anaemia or pulmonary vascular disease; a normal or high DLCO can occur in asthma and some extrapulmonary restrictive disorders.
- Evaluate **VA** and **KCO (DLCO/VA)** with the mechanism rather than declaring a low DLCO diagnostic of fibrosis.

**Bronchodilator responsiveness:**

- The 2022 ERS/ATS standard defines a significant change as an increase of **>10% of the predicted value** in FEV₁ or FVC, rather than simply a 12%/200 mL increase from baseline (the latter is the older convention still encountered in reports).
- A positive response supports reversible airflow limitation but does not establish asthma by itself; a negative single test does not exclude asthma.
- In a patient with low lung volumes, clarify whether change in FVC reflects reduced gas trapping rather than an increase in airway calibre alone.

**Exam-style interpretation:**

- A patient has FEV₁ 1.1 L (40% predicted), FVC 2.4 L (67% predicted), FEV₁/FVC 0.46, TLC 115% predicted, RV 175% predicted and DLCO 43% predicted.
- This is **obstruction with marked air trapping and impaired gas transfer**, supporting emphysema-predominant COPD in the right clinical setting—not restriction merely because FVC is low.
- By contrast, a patient with FEV₁/FVC 0.85, FVC 55%, TLC 58% and DLCO 42% has confirmed restriction with gas-transfer impairment, prompting investigation for ILD; assess CT and functional reserve before anaesthesia.

**Perioperative meaning:**

- PFTs classify mechanics and disease severity but should not alone dictate whether a patient can have non-thoracic surgery.
- Interpret with exercise capacity, resting oxygenation, hypercapnia, recent exacerbation, frailty and surgery.
- For lung resection, predicted postoperative FEV₁ and DLCO and exercise testing are more relevant than baseline spirometry alone.
- Source: [ERS/ATS interpretative technical standard, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.01499-2021).

## 1.6 Three blood-gas patterns worth interpreting aloud

**Pattern A — pneumonia/ARDS with respiratory alkalosis:**

- PH 7.49, PaCO₂ 3.8 kPa, PaO₂ 7.8 kPa on FiO₂ 0.5, HCO₃⁻ 21. The immediate problem is severe oxygenation failure (P/F ≈ 117 mmHg) despite vigorous alveolar ventilation.
- An elevated A–a gradient and inflammatory consolidation suggest shunt/V/Q mismatch, not a sedative-induced failure to breathe.
- Escalate oxygen support and search for cause; rising PaCO₂ later could signify fatigue and deterioration rather than improvement.

**Pattern B — opioid hypoventilation:**

- PH 7.21, PaCO₂ 9.2 kPa, PaO₂ 7.5 kPa on room air, HCO₃⁻ 27, low RR and pinpoint pupils.
- Pure alveolar hypoventilation typically produces an approximately normal A–a gradient.
- Oxygen may normalise SpO₂ while CO₂ continues to rise; restore airway ventilation, titrate naloxone to adequate breathing and ensure monitoring for recurrent sedation, especially with long-acting drugs.

**Pattern C — chronic COPD with acute sepsis:**

- PH 7.21, PaCO₂ 8.2 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 27, lactate 4.0.
- The bicarbonate is not as high as would be expected for a long-standing PaCO₂ of 8.2 kPa, suggesting either acute ventilatory deterioration or a simultaneous metabolic acidosis.
- Calculate the anion gap and compare with baseline gas; support ventilation while resuscitating sepsis.
- Do not label it simply “compensated type II failure”.

**Oxygenation indices and their limitations:**

- The P/F ratio is useful for trend and ARDS severity, but depends on FiO₂, PEEP, shunt and clinical state.
- The oxygenation index OI = mean airway pressure × FiO₂ × 100 / PaO₂(mmHg) also incorporates support intensity (widely used in paediatrics/ECMO selection).
- A high PEEP may improve P/F by recruiting lung but worsen perfusion; assess haemodynamics and driving pressure alongside any index.
- Arterial gases offer precise PaO₂/PaCO₂ but are a snapshot; serial observation and objective work of breathing are essential.

## 1.7 More on shunt, dead space and physiological tests

- A **shunt fraction** can be conceptualised by Qs/Qt = (Cc'O₂ − CaO₂)/(Cc'O₂ − CvO₂), where Cc' is ideal end-capillary oxygen content.
- Large shunts disproportionately reduce PaO₂ despite high FiO₂, but actual shunt estimation requires mixed venous blood, FiO₂ context and assumptions.
- In practice use response to oxygen, imaging, echo and clinical cause rather than ordering formal shunt fraction in every hypoxaemic patient.

- The **Bohr dead-space equation** (VD/VT = (PACO₂−PECO₂)/PACO₂, using alveolar PACO₂) explains why minute ventilation may fail to clear CO₂ in PE/ARDS.
- The Enghoff modification substitutes arterial PaCO₂ and captures both true dead space and broader V/Q inequality/shunt contributions; it should not be described as purely anatomical dead space.
- If PaCO₂ is 50 and mixed expired CO₂ 25 mmHg, calculated ratio 0.5 means half of each breath is effectively wasted for CO₂ elimination under those assumptions.

**Capnography:**

- ETCO₂ usually falls when pulmonary blood flow falls abruptly; in healthy lungs PaCO₂ exceeds ETCO₂ slightly, but in severe dead-space disease the gap can widen substantially.
- High ETCO₂ can reflect hypoventilation or excess production; a normal ETCO₂ does **not** always mean normal PaCO₂ in a severely shocked or obstructed patient.
- For a ventilated patient whose ABG shows PaCO₂ 70 and ETCO₂ 37, increasing ventilation without addressing dead space or pulmonary perfusion may be ineffective and dangerous.

items.body:
## 2.1 The immediate problem-solving sequence

The ANZCA emergency outcome asks not simply for a differential, but for relative likelihood, severity, appropriate immediate action and definitive treatment. **Prioritise actions before naming the final diagnosis.**

- **1.** **Call for help**, tell surgeon to pause, turn FiO₂ to 1.0, confirm pulse/ECG/BP and look at SpO₂, ETCO₂, tidal volumes and pressures together.

- **2.** **Check the airway and circuit:** oxygen supply/flow, source and bag, circuit disconnection, kink/filter, tube depth, cuff, obstruction, oesophageal or endobronchial position. Disconnect from ventilator and hand-ventilate with a known source when necessary; check suction-catheter passage.

- **3.** **Examine the patient:** both sides of chest, bronchospasm, crepitations, neck/chest swelling, skin, haemodynamics, blood loss, anaesthetic depth.

- **4.** **Treat immediately reversible causes** (e.g. remove obstruction, withdraw a mainstem tube, bronchodilator, decompress suspected tension pneumothorax, reverse residual block/opioid where appropriate); add ultrasound/ABG/CXR once safe.

- **5.** **Reassess continually:** improvement in SpO₂ alone is insufficient if ETCO₂ and ventilation deteriorate.

- **Exam trap:** an abrupt fall in ETCO₂ with hypotension is more suspicious for sudden reduced pulmonary blood flow (PE, arrest, severe low output) than for isolated hypoventilation, which generally raises ETCO₂ after equilibration. A flat capnogram can also mean disconnection/oesophageal intubation or cessation of ventilation.

## 2.2 Hypoxaemia during anaesthesia and postoperative dyspnoea

- Common causes are **atelectasis, V/Q mismatch, airway/tube problems, obesity/FRC reduction and inadequate oxygen delivery**.
- Less common but immediately life-threatening: aspiration, severe bronchospasm, tension pneumothorax, PE, pulmonary oedema and airway loss.
- Under GA, FRC decreases, dependent lung collapses, HPV may be impaired, and positioning or pneumoperitoneum further reduces compliance.

| **Pattern** | **Most useful clue** | **Immediate decision** |
|---|---|---|
| Low SpO₂ + high peak pressure | Obstruction, bronchospasm, reduced compliance, pneumothorax | Hand-ventilate, compare plateau/peak, examine and ultrasound |
| Low SpO₂ + low/absent ETCO₂ | Disconnection, oesophageal tube, arrest/PE | Verify airway/tube and perfusion immediately |
| Low SpO₂ after turning/laparoscopy | Mainstem tube, atelectasis, pneumothorax, FRC loss | Check tube depth, PEEP, position, insufflation pressure |
| Low SpO₂ + crackles/secretions | Aspiration, oedema, infection | Suction, oxygen/PEEP, echo/LUS, treat cause |
| Post-extubation stridor | Upper-airway oedema, laryngospasm, vocal cord dysfunction | Airway manoeuvres, CPAP, treat obstruction; early reintubation if failing |

**Management ladder:**

- Ensure true oxygen delivery; airway patency → increase FiO₂ → optimise ventilation/PEEP and recruitment when haemodynamically tolerable → correct specific cause.
- For a spontaneously breathing patient, use HFNC/CPAP/NIV according to phenotype and avoid an unsafe trial in a patient requiring immediate intubation.
- For severe oxygenation failure, refer to Chapter 5.

## 2.3 High airway pressures: resistance versus compliance

The airway pressure produced during inflation is a combination of **resistive** and **elastic** components plus PEEP. In a passive volume-controlled breath with inspiratory hold:

Ppeak − Pplat reflects flow-dependent airway/circuit resistance.

Pplat − PEEPtotal reflects elastic driving pressure; Cstat = VT / (Pplat − PEEPtotal).

If peak pressure rises but plateau stays relatively unchanged, think bronchospasm, secretions, kinked tube, blocked HME/filter or fast inspiratory flow. If both rise, think worsening compliance (atelectasis, pulmonary oedema, ARDS), pneumothorax, raised abdominal pressure or patient–ventilator dyssynchrony.

In pressure-controlled ventilation a compliance deterioration appears primarily as **lower delivered tidal volume**, not a high set pressure. Check for active patient effort: inspiratory holds and static compliance are unreliable when a patient is struggling against the ventilator.

**Immediate response:**

- FiO₂ 1.0, pause surgery, inspect circuit/tube/filter and endobronchial position, suction, manual ventilation, auscultate and examine for asymmetric expansion, decompress if tension physiology.
- Treat wheeze with inhaled salbutamol ± ipratropium and deeper anaesthesia; if silent with shock, consider life-threatening bronchospasm/anaphylaxis.
- Check plateau after the patient is passive and assess auto-PEEP with an expiratory hold when appropriate.
- Avoid repeatedly increasing inspiratory pressure without diagnosing the mechanism.

## 2.4 Hypercapnia and hypocapnia

- **Hypercapnia** may be due to reduced minute ventilation (drug effect, machine setting), increased dead space (PE, low flow, severe COPD), excess CO₂ load (fever, MH, CO₂ insufflation), rebreathing (exhausted soda lime, faulty unidirectional valve) or dynamic hyperinflation.
- Rising ETCO₂ with rising airway pressures after insufflation suggests CO₂ absorption plus restricted ventilation; an abrupt ETCO₂ rise with tachycardia, rigidity and hyperthermia raises malignant hyperthermia concern.
- Confirm PaCO₂ on ABG, because PaCO₂–ETCO₂ gap widens with dead space and low pulmonary perfusion.

Treat airway/ventilator cause, increase effective alveolar ventilation **without injurious volume/pressure**, correct rebreathing, manage temperature and metabolism. In severe obstruction, chasing normal PaCO₂ by increasing rate may aggravate auto-PEEP and hypotension; permissive hypercapnia can be safer if pH and contraindications allow.

- **Hypocapnia** generally reflects excessive alveolar ventilation, anxiety/pain, early hypoxaemic drive, PE, pregnancy or iatrogenic overventilation.
- Consequences include cerebral vasoconstriction/↓ CBF, left shift of oxyhaemoglobin curve, ↓ ionised calcium and arrhythmia susceptibility.
- Check whether low ETCO₂ represents **low PaCO₂** (true hyperventilation) or **low pulmonary perfusion** (PE, shock).
- Reduce unnecessary minute ventilation, treat the cause, and avoid reflexive ventilation changes during haemodynamic collapse.

## 2.5 Aspiration of gastric contents

- Aspiration causes **chemical pneumonitis** (acid/particulate epithelial injury), **mechanical obstruction** and/or **bacterial aspiration pneumonia**.
- Severity depends on volume, pH, particulate burden, host defence and coexisting lung disease.
- Sudden bronchospasm, desaturation, high pressures, visible gastric material or new dependent infiltrates may occur during induction, airway management or emergence.

**Immediate sequence:**

- Inform surgeon, position/suction oropharynx, secure a cuffed tube if required, suction trachea via tube, give FiO₂ 1.0 and appropriate PEEP, bronchodilate when wheezing; treat severe lung injury supportively with lung-protective ventilation.
- Remove large obstructing solids via bronchoscopy; routine lavage of acidic aspirate is not proven and can spread injury.
- **Do not prescribe prophylactic antibiotics or corticosteroids for uncomplicated sterile chemical aspiration.** Give antibiotics if there is established/suspected bacterial infection or clinically convincing evolution to pneumonia; initially monitor progression, imaging and gas exchange.
- Consider ARDS evolution and postoperative ICU disposition if severe.

Prevent by risk-stratified fasting, assessing obstruction/full stomach, safe RSI where indicated, aspiration precautions and airway protection. Gastric ultrasound may add information in selected equivocal cases but cannot eliminate clinical judgment. Do not use a fixed aspirate-volume cutoff as a bedside prediction of severity.

## 2.6 Severe bronchospasm during general anaesthesia

- Common causes include asthma/COPD, airway instrumentation at light anaesthesia, ETT kink/secretions or aspiration; always consider **anaphylaxis** when hypotension, rash or temporal drug association coexists.
- Typical waveforms: prolonged expiration, “shark-fin” capnogram, high peak–plateau gradient, wheeze, reduced expiratory flow; **silent chest may signify almost no airflow**.

- **1.** FiO₂ 1.0, call for help, check tube/circuit and exclude endobronchial tube, anaphylaxis and pneumothorax.

- **2.** Deepen anaesthesia (propofol or volatile agent as haemodynamics allow), avoid airway stimulation; hand-ventilate gently.

- **3.** Give inhaled **salbutamol** (e.g. 4–10 puffs via suitable in-circuit spacer, repeated, or nebulised 5 mg) and **ipratropium 0.5 mg** for severe episodes. Systemic corticosteroids early, noting delayed benefit.

- **4.** For severe/refractory episodes consider **IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over ≈20 minutes** and carefully titrated IV bronchodilator or adrenaline when clinically appropriate; **adrenaline is first-line for anaphylaxis**, not automatically for uncomplicated asthma.

- **5.** Reduce respiratory rate, lengthen expiratory time, assess auto-PEEP, accept some hypercapnia; manage hypotension from dynamic hyperinflation by brief circuit disconnection/exhalation where appropriate and restoration of perfusion.

These adult drug examples require adjustment for patient/setting. See Chapter 6 for status asthmaticus physiology and post-crisis management.

## 2.7 Pneumothorax and tension pneumothorax

- Air enters the pleural space, separating pleura and collapsing lung.
- **Tension physiology** occurs when rising intrapleural pressure obstructs venous return and reduces cardiac output; it is a clinical emergency, not a radiographic descriptor.
- Causes include ventilation barotrauma, CVC insertion, trauma and underlying bullous disease.
- Signs may be sudden high airway pressure, hypoxaemia, unilateral reduced breath sounds, expanding chest, hypotension or arrest.
- Tracheal deviation and distended neck veins are late/unreliable.

- **Diagnosis:** In an unstable ventilated patient, treat suspected tension pneumothorax immediately—do not delay for CXR. Lung ultrasound: absent sliding has alternative causes; absence of B-lines/lung pulse supports; lung point is highly specific when seen but may disappear in complete collapse. Supine CXR may show deep sulcus; CT is most sensitive in stable patients.

**Management:**

- Relieve pressure urgently with **finger thoracostomy or needle decompression** as appropriate to context, anatomy, equipment and training; in unstable traumatic patients or when needle reliability is poor, finger thoracostomy is preferred by many Australasian trauma protocols.
- Insert a definitive intercostal drain where required, with ultrasound guidance for nonemergency pleural procedures and safe-site technique.
- For positive-pressure ventilation with a clinically important pneumothorax, involve surgical/critical-care colleagues about drainage rather than relying on oxygen alone.
- Treat open chest wound, bronchopleural fistula and ongoing air leak as separate problems.

**Chest drain safety:**

- Confirm side and indication, control analgesia, use asepsis and appropriate intercostal site, blunt dissection for surgical drain, avoid inferior rib neurovascular bundle, and ensure water seal/underwater drainage and a plan for suction if needed.
- Do not clamp a bubbling drain without specialist reason; monitor for re-expansion pulmonary oedema and catheter malposition.

### What changes with stable, ventilated and tension pneumothorax?

- A pneumothorax is pleural air that separates visceral and parietal pleura.
- **The immediate danger is determined by physiology, not by the radiographic size alone**.
- Spontaneous breathing can permit a selected small, stable pneumothorax to be observed under a defined pathway, whereas positive-pressure ventilation can enlarge an air leak rapidly.
- Tension physiology raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and causes obstructive shock; it is a **clinical emergency**, not a diagnosis that requires a particular mediastinal-shift appearance on CXR.

| **Situation** | **Key findings** | **Decision** |
|---|---|---|
| Stable, spontaneously breathing | Mild symptoms, maintained oxygenation/perfusion; no progressive physiological compromise | Observation/aspiration/drain according to cause, size, symptoms and local pleural pathway; reassess before elective anaesthesia. |
| Pneumothorax with positive-pressure ventilation | Rising peak/plateau pressure, falling saturation, reduced compliance; may be occult on supine CXR | Urgent bedside assessment; involve senior/surgical team for drain planning, particularly if clinically important or progressing. A tiny stable occult traumatic pneumothorax may be managed selectively under closely monitored specialist protocols, not by a blanket rule. |
| Suspected tension pneumothorax | Sudden hypoxaemia, severe hypotension/PEA, unilateral ventilation signs, rising airway pressure | **Immediate decompression without waiting for imaging**, then definitive pleural drainage and reassessment. |

**Procedure choice and pitfalls:**

- In a critically unstable trauma patient, finger thoracostomy in an appropriate intercostal space is often more reliable than a short cannula and may be preferred in Australasian resuscitation settings where trained operators are available.
- Needle decompression can be lifesaving where it is the immediately available intervention, but may fail due to chest-wall thickness, inappropriate length or kinking; reassess response and proceed to definitive drainage.
- Do not force routine diagnostic imaging before decompression.
- With bilateral compromise or arrest after trauma, consider bilateral chest decompression within the trauma arrest pathway.
- For non-emergency drainage use ultrasound and the safest site for the indication; avoid blindly placing an intercostal drain below the diaphragm or through the neurovascular bundle.
- Check tube function (air leak, oscillation, drainage system), ongoing bronchopleural fistula and new re-expansion oedema.

**Worked peri-anaesthetic situation:**

- After laparoscopic insufflation, peak pressure rises from 22 to 39 cmH₂O, SpO₂ falls and BP becomes 65/35 with near-absent left air entry.
- Give FiO₂ 1.0, stop insufflation, check tube/circuit and hand-ventilate.
- If instability and unilateral findings remain compatible with tension, **decompress immediately**; do not wait for a plateau-pressure measurement, ultrasound or CXR to become available.
- Afterwards insert/confirm a drain, investigate the source and plan postoperative monitoring.
- Local trauma and pleural protocols govern detailed site/device selection.

## 2.8 Respiratory arrest: resuscitation and critical evaluation (SS_IC 1.64)

Respiratory arrest is absent or ineffective ventilation, potentially **before cardiac arrest**. A palpable pulse does not imply adequate oxygen delivery to the brain. Causes include airway obstruction, opioids/sedatives, residual neuromuscular block, neuromuscular disease, severe asthma, intracranial catastrophe, pulmonary pathology and circuit failure.

**With a pulse:**

- Call emergency help; establish airway opening, suction/adjuncts, give bag–mask ventilation with oxygen, assess chest rise and CO₂, rapidly restore an advanced airway when needed.
- Use a monitored, appropriately paced rescue-breath strategy (in adults approximately one breath every 6 seconds when a pulse persists, adjusting for physiology and avoiding hyperventilation), and check pulse regularly.
- Treat cause: e.g. naloxone titrated for opioid toxicity without provoking abrupt withdrawal, sugammadex/neostigmine when appropriate to objectively confirmed neuromuscular blockade, remove obstructing foreign body, manage severe bronchospasm.

**If no pulse:**

- Initiate high-quality CPR and ANZCOR adult ALS: chest compressions, defibrillation of shockable rhythms, oxygenation and ventilation, and correction of reversible causes.
- With a secure advanced airway, avoid interrupting compressions for ventilation and avoid excessive minute ventilation.
- In severe asthma, auto-PEEP may make compressions and venous return ineffective; briefly release trapped gas and resume with a lower respiratory rate.
- For tension pneumothorax, relieve the obstruction; for suspected massive PE in arrest, consider condition-specific reperfusion with specialist team.

**Critical evaluation:**

- Bag-mask is rapid and versatile but depends on seal/patency and risks gastric insufflation
- Supraglottic devices can rescue ventilation but do not reliably protect against aspiration
- Intubation secures the airway but can delay oxygenation or cause haemodynamic collapse.
- Choose the fastest effective oxygenation method, not intubation at any cost.
- Excessive ventilation reduces cerebral/coronary perfusion by increasing intrathoracic pressure; capnography is invaluable for tube confirmation, ventilation trends and detecting possible ROSC, but ETCO₂ is also influenced by perfusion.

### Respiratory arrest: decision-making under physiological uncertainty

- The first distinction is **apnoea with a pulse versus cardiac arrest**.
- In apnoea with a pulse the immediate treatment is **effective assisted ventilation**, not chest compression.
- Deliver oxygen by bag–mask using a two-person seal, jaw thrust, suction and an adjunct where indicated; observe chest rise, use continuous capnography if available and reassess pulse frequently.
- A supraglottic airway may rescue ventilation when mask seal is poor; a tracheal tube is appropriate when repeated ventilation is needed, the airway is unprotected or ventilation is failing.
- Do not postpone oxygenation while preparing a theoretically more definitive device.

| **Cause** | **Clues** | **Cause-specific action after immediate airway/ventilation support** |
|---|---|---|
| Opioid or sedative effect | Bradypnoea, low minute ventilation, consciousness reduction; potentially recurrent with long-acting drug | Ventilate first; titrate naloxone for opioid effect to adequate spontaneous respiration, observe for resedation. Benzodiazepine reversal is highly selected because flumazenil may precipitate seizures/withdrawal. |
| Residual neuromuscular blockade | Shallow breaths, upper-airway obstruction, weak cough; subjective head lift is unreliable | Objective TOF monitoring; give appropriate reversal (sugammadex for suitable aminosteroid blockade or neostigmine when appropriate) while continuing ventilation. |
| Upper-airway obstruction/laryngospasm | Stridor, absent air movement despite chest effort, poor capnogram | Jaw thrust, CPAP/oxygen, remove stimulation/suction when safe, deepen anaesthesia; early NMBA and intubation if sustained/complete obstruction. |
| Critical asthma | Silent chest, prolonged expiration, auto-PEEP, hypotension after intubation | Bronchodilate, lower minute ventilation demand, allow trapped gas to exhale, exclude pneumothorax/anaphylaxis; do not rapidly bag at high rates. |
| Neuromuscular/bulbar failure | Weak cough, aspiration risk, paradoxical breathing; chronic symptoms may be subtle | Assisted ventilation and controlled airway protection; assess bulbar and secretion burden and plan prolonged support. |
| PE/tension pneumothorax or cardiac arrest | Abrupt loss of perfusion/ETCO₂, collapse | Start ANZCOR ALS if pulseless, treat obstructive cause immediately; consider PE reperfusion pathway with bleeding risk. |

**Ventilation strategy and critical evaluation:**

- Avoid excessive tidal volume or rate in the resuscitation phase—gastric insufflation, aspiration and increased intrathoracic pressure impair venous return.
- With an advanced airway during cardiac arrest, deliver breaths without pausing compressions, following current ANZCOR ALS rhythm and ventilation recommendations; use ETCO₂ as a trend rather than a standalone measure of CPR quality or a reason to stop resuscitation.
- Pulse checks should be brief.
- After restoring ventilation assess an ABG, neurological recovery, aspiration risk and whether recurrent hypoventilation mandates ICU/HDU.
- Consider extubation only after full return of airway reflexes, neuromuscular function, and a safe ventilation plan.

**Viva framing:**

- Compare bag–mask (fast but mask seal/aspiration limitations), supraglottic device (rapid hands-free ventilation but less airway protection) and intubation (secure route but induction and prolonged attempt risks).
- The correct choice is the **fastest effective airway that can be sustained safely**.
- This is a critical evaluation of the method and its consequences, not merely a recall of the ALS algorithm.
- Source: [ANZCOR resuscitation guidance](https://www.anzcor.org/home/).

## 2.9 A structured respiratory crisis decision table

| **Situation** | **First 30 seconds** | **First 5 minutes** | **Definitive plan** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sudden desaturation with high pressures | FiO₂ 1; call for help; manual ventilation; tube/circuit check | Compare peak/plateau; auscultate; suction; LUS for pneumothorax; treat bronchospasm | Correct cause, reassess ventilation/ABG, postoperative disposition |
| Low ETCO₂ plus shock | Confirm pulse, tube/circuit, oxygenation; initiate ALS if pulseless | Echo for RV/other cardiac failure, assess haemorrhage, PE, tension, anaphylaxis | Reperfusion, decompression, blood products or anaphylaxis algorithm as diagnosis dictates |
| Rising CO₂ during laparoscopy | Confirm equipment and CO₂ absorber; check ventilation/pressures | Reduce pneumoperitoneum, adjust MV safely, exclude MH if sudden unexplained rise | Correct root cause, ABG and core temperature, stop trigger if MH |
| Patient cannot breathe after extubation | Jaw thrust, oxygen/CPAP, assess obstruction | Manage laryngospasm, reverse residual neuromuscular blockade, assess NPPE/aspiration | Reintubate if failing; PACU/ICU monitoring and prevention |
| Severe unilateral chest findings with shock | Suspect tension immediately | Decompress without imaging delay | Drain, confirm expansion and seek source of air leak |

**The highest-scoring viva approach is causal.** It is not enough to say “give oxygen and a bronchodilator”: explain whether the immediate hazard is airway patency, gas exchange, alveolar ventilation or circulatory collapse. The first physical action is determined by which failure threatens life first; investigations confirm and refine management rather than delay rescue.

items.body:
## 3.1 Why support must match the mechanism

![Matching non-invasive support to the physiological failure](set3-fig3.png)

- The aim of support is not merely to improve saturation; it is to **reduce respiratory muscle work, correct the physiological defect and prevent deterioration without delaying necessary intubation**.
- Oxygen raises inspired oxygen concentration, but does not reverse fatigue or provide a reliable tidal volume.
- Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) recruits alveoli and counteracts upper-airway collapse.
- Bilevel non-invasive ventilation (NIV) adds inspiratory pressure to unload muscles and increase alveolar ventilation.
- Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) provides reliable high FiO₂, washes upper-airway dead space and offers mild variable positive pressure—but is not equivalent to pressure-supported ventilation.

| **Device** | **What is delivered** | **Principal benefit** | **Main limitation and best use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard oxygen (nasal prongs/mask) | Supplemental FiO₂, variable depending on flow and respiratory pattern | Mild hypoxaemia | Does not reduce high work of breathing or ventilatory failure |
| HFNC | Warm humidified high flow often 30–60 L/min; FiO₂ titrated 0.21–1.0 | Hypoxaemia, secretion tolerance, limited dead-space washout | Unreliable pressure support; failure must not delay intubation |
| CPAP | Single continuous pressure e.g. 5–10 cmH₂O | Recruitment, afterload unloading in cardiogenic oedema, upper-airway splinting | Does not actively assist inspiration; may impair venous return |
| Bilevel NIV (IPAP/EPAP) | Higher inspiratory than expiratory pressure; pressure support = IPAP–EPAP | Treats hypercapnic respiratory acidosis, reduces diaphragmatic work | Leak, poor synchrony, aspiration risk, requires cooperation and close observation |
| Invasive ventilation | Secured airway, reliable FiO₂, PEEP and controlled/assisted ventilation | Shock, severe exhaustion, failed non-invasive treatment, unsafe airway | Intubation/anaesthesia risks, VILI, VAP and delirium |

**2026 ATS update:**

- For de novo hypoxaemic failure, HFNC is recommended over standard oxygen (strong), while NIV or CPAP may be considered with close monitoring (conditional).
- For acute hypercapnic failure, facemask NIV remains first line (strong); HFNC is an alternative only in selected mild acidaemia (about pH >7.25) with close monitoring and immediate escalation available.
- After extubation, HFNC or NIV can reduce reintubation, with **NIV favoured in high-risk patients**.
- These are more current than older blanket statements that all hypoxaemic patients must receive NIV.

## 3.2 Starting NIV: assessment and first settings

**Best-supported indications:**

- Acute COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis (e.g. pH ≤7.35 and PaCO₂ >6 kPa after initial medical therapy); obesity hypoventilation with acute-on-chronic hypercapnia; selected neuromuscular/chest-wall disease; cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (CPAP or NIV).
- NIV can also support selected immunocompromised or postextubation patients, but evidence and risks differ.
- De novo severe hypoxaemic ARDS on NIV has a substantial risk of delayed intubation and patient-self-inflicted lung injury from very high inspiratory effort.

**Relative/absolute barriers:**

- Respiratory arrest, inability to protect airway, uncontrolled vomiting/active aspiration, severe agitation without safe tolerance, severe facial trauma/impossible interface, copious uncontrolled secretions or haemodynamic collapse requiring urgent intubation.
- A reduced GCS from pure hypercapnic encephalopathy is not invariably an absolute contraindication in a closely monitored expert environment with immediate airway capability; reassess the response rapidly.

**Example starting bilevel NIV for AECOPD:**

- Suitable full-face interface; EPAP ≈4–5 cmH₂O and IPAP ≈10–15 cmH₂O, then progressively increase IPAP to achieve adequate chest expansion, lower respiratory rate, better comfort and improving pH/PaCO₂.
- EPAP may be increased for severe oxygenation problems or OSA/upper-airway collapse, but excessive EPAP can worsen hyperinflation and trigger difficulties in COPD; adjust pressure support accordingly.
- Titrate oxygen to SpO₂ **88–92%** when at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
- Check mask fit, leak, synchrony, trigger sensitivity and circuit exhalation port—do not occlude a required exhaust valve.

- **Monitor within 30–60 min** and repeat gas within about 1–2 hours depending on severity.
- Improvement means RR/effort falls, pH rises, PaCO₂ and clinical status improve, and oxygen requirement stabilises.
- **Do not simply continue NIV because the SpO₂ is higher** if mental state, work, haemodynamics or pH deteriorate.
- Prolonged low-quality NIV can worsen aspiration risk and delay a safer, controlled intubation.

## 3.3 Choosing HFNC and CPAP intelligently

- HFNC works well in acute hypoxaemic failure because it can match high inspiratory demand and reduce entrainment of room air, improving effective FiO₂.
- Start with sufficiently high flow (often ≈40–60 L/min in adults with major distress, as tolerated), adjust FiO₂ to the clinical oxygen target and reduce flow when work settles.
- Look at the trajectory: persistent RR >30, rising FiO₂ requirement, exhaustion or haemodynamic deterioration should prompt early senior review.
- A ROX index (SpO₂/FiO₂) / RR may support prediction in selected populations (higher is generally reassuring), but no single cutoff is a substitute for close clinical assessment.

- CPAP is useful for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema by recruiting lung, lowering inspiratory effort and reducing LV transmural afterload; start around 5–10 cmH₂O and titrate.
- Avoid assuming all patients tolerate positive pressure: severe RV failure, obstructive shock, marked hypovolaemia and untreated pneumothorax can worsen dramatically.
- For OSA, reinstitute the patient's known CPAP where possible rather than guessing a therapeutic pressure.

## 3.4 Intubation in critically ill respiratory failure

- **Why induction is dangerous:** removing sympathetic tone can collapse vascular resistance; apnoea rapidly desaturates an already low-FRC lung; positive pressure can impair RV preload and worsen obstructive disease; a first-pass failure is more costly than in an elective patient.

- Before induction, coordinate roles, equipment and rescue plans
- Position head-up if possible
- Choose preoxygenation with **HFNC or NIV** (supported by 2026 ATS recommendations), use bag-mask/PEEP where appropriate, prepare two suction systems for secretions/aspiration, consider awake techniques when indicated by airway difficulty, ensure invasive BP/vasopressor readiness if unstable, and optimise volume only if genuinely deficient.
- Etomidate, ketamine or reduced-dose titrated propofol/other agents may be selected according to physiology; no agent is universally haemodynamically safe.
- Use appropriate neuromuscular blockade and confirm tube with sustained waveform capnography.

After intubation:

- Verify tube depth and bilateral ventilation.
- Reduce FiO₂ to a safe target.
- Start lung-protective settings based on **predicted**, not actual, body weight.
- Use PEEP appropriately.
- Monitor ABG, plateau, driving pressure, auto-PEEP, haemodynamics and sedation requirements.

- In severe bronchospasm or OHS, avoid a high-rate default that induces gas trapping.
- In severe ARDS, prioritise protection over complete normalisation of PaCO₂.

## 3.5 NIV and HFNC failure: avoid the false reassurance trap

- An increasing SpO₂ after NIV does not imply success if tidal breathing remains laboured.
- **Failure signals** include worsening acidosis, rising PaCO₂, persistent high respiratory rate, declining consciousness, worsening secretions/aspiration, intolerance, refractory hypoxaemia, or hypotension.
- Assess at the bedside soon after initiation and set a documented escalation time; do not keep repeatedly tightening the mask or increasing pressures for hours without judging whether the underlying condition is improving.

**Asynchrony:**

- With COPD, auto-PEEP creates an inspiratory threshold load before the patient can trigger the ventilator.
- Too-insensitive triggers cause ineffective efforts; excessively sensitive triggers cause auto-triggering from leaks.
- High leak also compromises delivered pressure and measurements.
- Adjust mask, trigger, pressure support, rise time and cycling while watching the patient and pressure/flow curves.
- Dynamic hyperinflation may worsen if inspiratory time is too long; earlier cycling can increase expiratory time.
- When IPAP increases with fixed EPAP, the pressure-support difference increases, often helping CO₂ clearance; when both rise equally, inspiratory unloading may not improve.

**Intubation versus NIV in high-risk physiology:**

- Shock, vomiting, inability to protect airway or impending arrest may preclude safe NIV.
- Conversely, hypercapnic COPD with pH around 7.27, stable haemodynamics and intact airway protection is precisely where a supported NIV trial can avoid an invasive airway.
- Successful use requires skilled staff, gas reassessment, accessible intubation and realistic goals-of-care conversations.

## 3.6 Interface choice and practical errors with noninvasive support

**Masks:**

- An oronasal/full-face mask commonly achieves better pressure delivery in acute hypercapnic distress than nasal-only interfaces, but causes claustrophobia, facial pressure injury and risk if vomiting.
- A helmet may permit higher tolerated PEEP and less facial pressure in experienced centres but needs attention to CO₂ rebreathing, fresh gas flow and synchrony.
- Fit and leak affect delivered pressure as much as the set IPAP/EPAP; a poorly fitting interface can create falsely reassuring displayed settings.

**Common errors:**

- Inadequate EPAP with severe OSA/airway collapse, excessive EPAP that worsens COPD hyperinflation, low IPAP–EPAP difference failing to unload a tired patient, aggressive sedation that masks failure, inadequate staff observations and delaying intubation despite progressive acidosis.
- For cardiogenic oedema, CPAP may be sufficient because recruitment and LV afterload reduction are central.
- For pure neuromuscular hypoventilation, bilevel support with an appropriate backup rate is more logical than CPAP, which does not provide effective inspiratory ventilation.

- **Why airways matter:** a patient with facial trauma, massive aspiration, uncontrolled haemoptysis or absent airway reflexes cannot be made safe by improving mask oxygenation. Decide who will intubate, which rescue airway is available, the preoxygenation strategy and the time limit for observing non-invasive treatment before initiating it.
